tagline: Paul's letter to a gifted, divided, and very Roman church, answering its quarrels and questions with the message of Christ crucified and risen.
overview:
First Corinthians is a real letter written to a real congregation with real problems, and that is what makes it so useful. The church in Corinth was only a few years old. It was rich in spiritual gifts and eloquent speech, and it was coming apart. Members were lining up behind favorite leaders, suing one another in pagan courts, tolerating a scandalous sexual relationship, arguing about marriage and celibacy, eating in pagan temples, humiliating poorer members at the Lord's Supper, competing over spiritual gifts, and doubting the resurrection of the body. Paul answers each problem in turn, first the troubles he has heard about by report, then the questions the Corinthians had put to him in a letter of their own.

What holds the letter together is not a list of rules but a single center. Paul keeps bringing every issue back to the cross, where God showed his wisdom and power in what the world counted weakness and foolishness, and to the resurrection, where God showed that the body and the future matter. Along the way the letter gives the church some of its most loved and most used passages: the account of the Lord's Supper in chapter 11, the picture of the church as one body with many members in chapter 12, the chapter on love in chapter 13, and the earliest written summary of the gospel and the resurrection appearances in chapter 15.

The letter matters because the Corinthian church looks so much like churches in every age. It was proud of its knowledge and blind to its divisions. It mixed the gospel with the status games of its city. Paul does not abandon the congregation, and he does not flatter it. He calls it holy while telling it plainly where it has gone wrong, which is a model of pastoral honesty in its own right.
author: The letter names Paul as its author, with "our brother Sosthenes" as co-sender (1:1). Paul's authorship is not seriously disputed by scholars of any school; 1 Corinthians belongs to the small group of letters that nearly everyone accepts as Paul's own. It is also one of the earliest Christian writings to be quoted by name: the letter known as 1 Clement, sent from the church in Rome to the church in Corinth around AD 96, reminds the Corinthians of what the apostle Paul had written to them about factions. Sosthenes may be the synagogue ruler of that name who was beaten in Corinth in Acts 18:17, though the name was common and the identification cannot be proved. Paul dictated at least part of the letter, since he adds a greeting in his own hand at the end (16:21). Some scholars have proposed that 1 Corinthians combines more than one of Paul's letters, but most regard it as a single letter, and its shifts of subject are explained by the fact that Paul is answering a list of separate questions.
date: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, on the west coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey), where he says he will stay "until Pentecost" (16:8). He had founded the Corinthian church a few years earlier, during a stay of about eighteen months described in Acts 18. That stay can be dated with unusual confidence, because Acts 18:12 says Paul was brought before Gallio, the Roman governor of Achaia, and an inscription found at Delphi places Gallio's term of office around AD 51 to 52. Paul then spent between two and three years in Ephesus (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31). First Corinthians comes from that period, most likely around AD 53 to 55. It was not Paul's first letter to the church: he mentions an earlier letter that has not survived (5:9). Second Corinthians, written later from Macedonia, shows that the relationship went through further strain after this letter was sent.
setting:
Corinth sat on the narrow isthmus that joins mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with a port on each side: Lechaeum on the Corinthian Gulf to the west and Cenchreae on the Saronic Gulf to the east. Cargo and even small ships were hauled across the isthmus on a paved trackway, so trade from east and west passed through the city. The old Greek city had been destroyed by the Roman general Lucius Mummius in 146 BC. In 44 BC Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony, settled largely with freed slaves and veterans, and it became the capital of the Roman province of Achaia. The Corinth that Paul knew was therefore a Roman city in Greece, laid out on Roman lines, with Latin as its official language and a population that included Greeks, Romans, Jews, and people from across the eastern Mediterranean.

It was a city where status could be won. Freedmen and merchants rose to wealth, sponsored public buildings, and had their generosity recorded in inscriptions; a paving stone near the theater records that an Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense in return for his office, and some identify him with the Erastus of Romans 16:23. The Isthmian Games, one of the great athletic festivals of Greece, were held nearby every two years. Temples to Apollo, Aphrodite, Asclepius the healing god, and the imperial family stood in and around the city, and meals in temple dining rooms were part of ordinary civic and social life. Orators and teachers of rhetoric drew crowds and followers. An often repeated claim that a temple of Aphrodite kept a thousand sacred prostitutes goes back to the geographer Strabo and describes the older Greek city; many historians doubt that it applied to Roman Corinth. What is clear is that the church Paul wrote to lived surrounded by idols, patronage, competition for honor, and a relaxed sexual ethic, and it had brought much of that world into its own gatherings.
purpose: Paul wrote to restore a divided church to the gospel it had received. He had heard reports from "Chloe's household" about quarrels (1:11) and other news about immorality and lawsuits (5:1; 6:1). He had also received a letter from the church asking a series of questions, and three members, Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, had come to him (16:17). The first part of the letter (chapters 1 to 6) deals with what he has heard. The second part answers the Corinthians' own questions, each introduced with the phrase "now concerning" or a close variant (7:1; 7:25; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1; 16:12). Through it all Paul aims at unity, holiness, and love: a church that builds up its weakest members instead of prizing its most impressive ones, and that waits for the resurrection rather than acting as if it had already arrived. He also prepares the church for the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (16:1-4) and for his coming visit.
story: The founding of the Corinthian church is told in Acts 18, during Paul's second missionary campaign. After preaching in Athens, Paul came to Corinth, worked as a tentmaker alongside Aquila and Priscilla, preached in the synagogue, and then moved next door to the house of Titius Justus when he met opposition. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believed with his household. After Paul left, the Alexandrian teacher Apollos ministered in Corinth (Acts 18:24-19:1). First Corinthians belongs to the next stage, Paul's long stay in Ephesus during his third campaign. In the larger story of the Bible, the letter shows the promise to Abraham reaching the nations: a church of Jews and Gentiles in a pagan Roman city, told “you yourselves are God’s temple” (3:16), learning what it means to be the holy people of God without a temple of stone, a land, or a king other than Christ.
christ: The letter is Christ-centered in the most literal way. Paul resolved to know nothing among the Corinthians "except Jesus Christ and Him crucified" (2:2), and the cross becomes the measure of wisdom, leadership, freedom, and worship. Christ is the foundation of the church (3:11), the Passover lamb who has been sacrificed (5:7), the one Lord through whom all things exist (8:6), the one whose body and blood the church shares at the Supper (10:16; 11:23-26), and the one whose body the believers are, each of them a member of it (12:12-27). Chapter 15 gives the fullest account in the New Testament of Christ's resurrection and its meaning: he died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many witnesses, and his resurrection is the firstfruits of the resurrection of all who belong to him. Christ is also the last Adam, the head of a new humanity, who will hand the kingdom over to the Father when every enemy, death included, is destroyed.
reading: Read 1 Corinthians as one side of a conversation. Paul sometimes quotes the Corinthians' own slogans before answering them, and many translations mark phrases such as "Everything is permissible for me" (6:12) as Corinthian sayings Paul is qualifying. Readers disagree about where some of these quotations begin and end, and those decisions shape the meaning of several passages. Pay attention to the division between the reports of chapters 1 to 6 and the "now concerning" questions from chapter 7 onward. Several topics, such as head coverings, the silence of women in 14:34-35 (which some manuscripts place after 14:40), speaking in tongues, and the meaning of baptism for the dead in 15:29, are genuinely difficult and disputed; the notes set out the main views. A common misreading takes the love chapter as a wedding reading detached from its setting. In context it is a rebuke to a church competing over spiritual gifts, and it describes the love that should govern worship and community life.

structure.title: Greeting and thanksgiving
structure.summary: Paul greets the church as God's holy people and thanks God for its gifts, while pointing ahead to the day of Christ that it must still wait for.

structure.title: Divisions and the wisdom of the cross
structure.summary: Paul answers the reports of factions gathered around leaders. The message of the crucified Christ overturns the world's wisdom and status, and leaders are only servants and stewards of God.

structure.title: Immorality, lawsuits, and the body
structure.summary: Paul confronts a case of incest the church has tolerated, rebukes members for suing one another before pagan courts, and teaches that the body belongs to the Lord and is a temple of the Holy Spirit.

structure.title: Marriage, singleness, and calling
structure.summary: Answering the Corinthians' first question, Paul discusses sexual relations within marriage, divorce, mixed marriages, and the value of remaining single in a time of pressure.

structure.title: Food offered to idols and the use of freedom
structure.summary: Paul addresses eating food sacrificed to idols. Knowledge must give way to love for the weaker brother, Paul gives up his own rights for the gospel, and the church must flee idolatry.

structure.title: Order in worship and the Lord's Supper
structure.summary: Paul addresses head coverings in worship and then rebukes the church for meals where the rich eat while the poor go hungry, handing on the tradition of the Lord's Supper.

structure.title: Spiritual gifts and the way of love
structure.summary: The Spirit gives varied gifts to one body for the common good. Love is the greater way, and worship should be orderly and intelligible so that everyone is built up.

structure.title: The resurrection of the dead
structure.summary: Paul restates the gospel of Christ's death, burial, resurrection, and appearances, argues that the resurrection of believers depends on it, and describes the resurrection body and the final defeat of death.

structure.title: The collection, travel plans, and greetings
structure.summary: Paul gives instructions for the collection for Jerusalem, shares his plans, commends coworkers, and closes with greetings in his own hand.

themes.title: The wisdom of the cross
themes.body: Corinth prized eloquence, knowledge, and status, and the church had carried those values into its life. Paul answers that God has shown his wisdom in a crucified Messiah, a message that looked foolish to Greeks and offensive to Jews. The cross does not only save; it reorders what counts as strength, honor, and wisdom, and Paul applies it to leadership, lawsuits, freedom, and worship.

themes.title: One body, one temple
themes.body: Paul describes the church as God's field, God's building, God's temple, and the body of Christ. These pictures all make the same point: the believers belong to God and to one another, and division is not a matter of taste but an attack on what God is building. Unity does not mean sameness; the body has many members with different gifts, and the weaker ones are indispensable.

themes.title: Holiness in the body
themes.body: Some Corinthians seem to have thought that what they did with their bodies did not touch their spiritual life. Paul insists the reverse. The body belongs to the Lord, is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and will be raised. Sexual conduct, food, and worship are therefore matters of holiness, and the church is called to be different from its city without withdrawing from it.

themes.title: Love that builds up
themes.body: Again and again Paul sets knowledge that puffs up against love that builds up. The strong are to limit their freedom for the sake of the weak, gifts are to serve the common good, and the Supper is to be shared, not hoarded. Chapter 13 gathers this theme into its most famous form: without love, even the most impressive gifts amount to nothing.

themes.title: Resurrection and the not yet
themes.body: Parts of the church behaved as if they had already arrived, rich and reigning. Paul reminds them that the end has not come: they still wait for the revelation of Christ, the day of judgment, and the resurrection of the body. Chapter 15 grounds Christian hope in Christ's bodily resurrection and makes it the reason that labor in the Lord is not in vain.

keyChapters.why: Sets out the letter's center: the message of the cross as God's power and wisdom, confronting a church divided by loyalty to leaders.
Leaders are servants and fellow workers, Christ is the only foundation, and the church is God's holy temple where his Spirit dwells.
Paul's longest discussion of marriage, singleness, and divorce, shaped by the conviction that the present form of the world is passing away.
On food sacrificed to idols, Paul sets knowledge against love and confesses one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ.
Contains the earliest written account of Jesus instituting the Lord's Supper, set in a rebuke of a divided church meal.
The Spirit gives varied gifts to one body for the common good, and every member, especially the weaker, is needed.
The chapter on love, which judges every gift and every claim to knowledge by whether it is patient, kind, and humble.
The fullest New Testament teaching on the resurrection of Christ and of believers, and the earliest written list of resurrection appearances.
